summary: An informal statement of discussion at the SJCC on moving data between sites. There are two problems: moving the data and interpreting it at the receiving end. The first needs a standard connection procedure and a standard packaging that lets the network collect a stream in order and know when a file ends.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 163 separates the task of moving data from the task of understanding it. It outlines a basic connection and packaging approach, while leaving file naming, interpretation and control for later discussion.

subtitle: An early discussion separating data movement from data interpretation.

tldr.problem: Moving data between sites and interpreting that data at the receiving site are separate problems.
tldr.mechanism: The note proposes a standard connection procedure and packaging that preserve order and indicate the end of a file, while leaving interpretation and control for later work.
tldr.outcome: It identifies protocol questions for a data transmission committee rather than specifying a complete transfer protocol.

today: RFC 163 is an informal protocol discussion published in May 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Two Data Transfer Problems
sections.content: This informal statement of discussion at the SJCC identifies two problems: moving data from one site to another, and interpreting the data at its destination. The RFC focuses on the first problem and explicitly leaves interpretation aside.
sections.plainLanguage: A receiving computer must get the data and understand what it means. This note focuses on how to move the data, not how to interpret it.

sections.title: Connection and Packaging
sections.content:
For file movement, the author proposes a standard connection procedure and standard packaging. The network should collect the transmitted stream in the right order and know when it reaches the end of a file. The Initial Connection Protocol is described as sufficient for connecting a serving Data Manager and a using process.

The note considers a Data Manager process at each host, as well as direct file transmission between processes. It raises possible ways to mark a file's end, including closing the connection after the last record.
sections.plainLanguage: A transfer needs a standard way to connect and a way to keep data in order and mark when a file ends. A host could use a Data Manager, or programs could connect directly.

sections.title: Naming and Control Are Separate
sections.content:
The note does not define how a process requests a named file or controls a transfer. A Data Manager would need a file name and other qualifiers to resolve access and naming questions. This information might travel in the data stream or on a separate control connection.

For direct process-to-process transfers, file naming and format interpretation are left to the processes. The RFC says a set of format and control protocols remains to be established.
sections.plainLanguage: The note does not decide how to name a file, check access or interpret its contents. Those details need separate rules above the basic transfer mechanism.
